title: Sleep and the Brain
hook: Sleep isn't the brain switching off — it's when the brain does some of its most important work, from clearing waste to locking in memories.
key_points: Sleep cycles between non-REM (deep, restorative) and REM (vivid dreaming) stages.
During sleep the brain consolidates memories, moving them into longer-term storage.
Sleep helps flush metabolic waste that builds up in the brain while awake.
Too little sleep impairs attention, mood, learning, and immune function.
The body's internal clock, the circadian rhythm, drives the sleep-wake cycle.
content_html: Sleep can look like the brain shutting down, but it's the opposite — some of the brain's most important work happens while you're unconscious. Over a night, the brain cycles between non-REM sleep, which includes the deep, restorative stages, and REM sleep, the stage of vivid dreams and intense brain activity. We spend roughly a third of our lives doing it, and no animal can skip it for long.
extra_html: The NIH's NINDS explains that sleep is far from passive. During the night the brain replays and consolidates the day's experiences, strengthening the connections that turn fleeting events into lasting memories. Sleep also appears to help flush out metabolic waste that builds up between neurons while you're awake. Driving all of this is the circadian rhythm — an internal clock, tuned by light, that schedules when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert. Skimp on sleep and the costs show up fast: blunted attention, low mood, poorer learning, and a weaker immune response.

related.title: The Brain
related.hook: Three pounds of folded tissue runs the whole show — thinking, balance, breathing, memory — divided into regions that each handle a different part of the job.

related.title: Memory and Learning
related.hook: Every memory you hold is a pattern of connections between neurons — and learning is, quite literally, your brain rewiring itself to make those connections stronger.

related.title: Neurons and Signals
related.hook: Your every thought, twitch, and feeling rides on tiny electrical pulses fired by neurons — and leaps the gaps between them as bursts of chemicals.

flashcards.prompt: Is the brain inactive during sleep?
flashcards.back_html: No — the brain is busy during sleep. It cycles through stages, consolidates memories, and clears out waste that piled up during the day.

flashcards.prompt: Which sleep stage is most associated with vivid dreaming?
flashcards.explanation_html: REM (rapid eye movement) sleep is when most vivid dreaming occurs and the brain is highly active even though the body's muscles are largely paralyzed.

flashcards.prompt: What is one well-supported function of sleep for the brain?

choices.text: Consolidating memories and clearing metabolic waste

flashcards.explanation_html: Sleep helps lock in memories and lets the brain clear waste products that accumulate during waking hours, among other restorative roles.
